title: Chapter 107 — The Carpenter
paragraphs: Seat yourself like a sultan among the moons of Saturn and take high, abstract man alone; and he seems a wonder, a grandeur, and a woe. But from the same point, take mankind in mass, and for the most part they seem a mob of unnecessary duplicates, both contemporary and hereditary. But most humble though he was, and far from furnishing an example of the high, humane abstraction, the Pequod's carpenter was no duplicate. Hence he now comes in person on this stage.

Like all sea-going ship carpenters, and more especially those belonging to whaling vessels, he was, to a certain casual, practical extent, experienced in numerous trades and callings related to his own — the carpenter's pursuit being the ancient and branching trunk of all those numerous crafts which more or less have to do with wood as a material. But besides the general observation above, this carpenter of the Pequod was singularly efficient in those thousand nameless mechanical emergencies continually arising on a large ship, upon a three- or four-year voyage in uncivilized and far-distant seas. For not to speak of his readiness in ordinary duties — repairing stove boats, sprung spars, reshaping clumsy-bladed oars, inserting porthole covers in the deck, or new tree-nails in the side planks, and other miscellaneous matters pertaining to his particular trade — he was moreover unhesitatingly expert in all manner of conflicting skills, both useful and whimsical.

The one grand stage where he performed all his manifold roles was his vice-bench: a long, crude, heavy table furnished with several vises of different sizes, both of iron and of wood. At all times except when whales were alongside, this bench was securely lashed crosswise against the rear of the try-works.

A belaying pin is found too large to be easily inserted into its hole: the carpenter claps it into one of his ever-ready vises and straightway files it smaller. A lost land-bird of strange plumage strays on board and is made a captive: out of clean-shaved rods of right-whale bone and crossbeams of sperm whale ivory, the carpenter makes a pagoda-looking cage for it. An oarsman sprains his wrist: the carpenter concocts a soothing lotion. Stubb longs for red stars to be painted upon the blade of his every oar; screwing each oar in his big wooden vise, the carpenter symmetrically supplies the constellation. A sailor takes a fancy to wear shark-bone earrings: the carpenter drills his ears. Another has a toothache: the carpenter pulls out pincers, and clapping one hand upon his bench bids him be seated there; but the poor fellow writhes uncontrollably under the unfinished operation; whirling round the handle of his wooden vise, the carpenter motions him to clamp his jaw in that, if he would have him draw the tooth.

Thus this carpenter was prepared at all points, and equally indifferent and disrespectful in all. Teeth he considered bits of ivory; heads he deemed but pulleys; men themselves he lightly regarded as capstans. But while, upon so wide a field, thus variously accomplished and with such liveliness of skill in him too, all this would seem to argue some uncommon quickness of intelligence. But not precisely so. For nothing was this man more remarkable than for a certain impersonal stolidity, as it were — impersonal, I say, for it so shaded off into the surrounding infinite of things that it seemed one with the general stolidity discernible in the whole visible world; which, while ceaselessly active in uncounted ways, still eternally holds its peace and ignores you, though you dig foundations for cathedrals. Yet was this half-horrible stolidity in him, involving too, as it appeared, an all-pervading heartlessness — yet was it oddly tinged at times with an old, crutch-like, antediluvian, wheezing humorousness, not without a certain grizzled wit. Such as might have served to pass the time during the midnight watch on the bearded forecastle of Noah's ark. Was it that this old carpenter had been a lifelong wanderer, whose much rolling to and fro had not only gathered no moss but, what is more, had rubbed off whatever small outward trappings might have originally belonged to him? He was a stripped abstraction; an undivided integer; uncompromised as a newborn babe; living without deliberate reference to this world or the next. You might almost say that this strange uncomplicatedness in him involved a sort of unconsciousness; for in his numerous trades, he did not seem to work so much by reason or by instinct, or simply because he had been trained to it, or by any mixture of all these; but merely by a kind of deaf-and-dumb, spontaneous literal process. He was a pure craftsman; his brain, if he had ever had one, must have early oozed into the muscles of his fingers. He was like one of those unreasoning but still highly useful Swiss Army knives, assuming the exterior — though a little swollen — of a common pocketknife but containing not only blades of various sizes but also screwdrivers, corkscrews, tweezers, awls, pens, rulers, nail-files, and countersinks. So if his superiors wanted to use the carpenter for a screwdriver, all they had to do was open that part of him and the screw was fast; or if for tweezers, take him up by the legs and there they were.

Yet, as previously hinted, this all-tooled, open-and-shut carpenter was, after all, no mere machine or automaton. If he did not have a common soul in him, he had a subtle something that somehow did its duty in an odd way. What that was — whether an essence of quicksilver or a few drops of smelling salts — there is no telling. But there it was, and there it had resided for now some sixty years or more. And this it was, this same unaccountable, cunning life-principle in him, that kept him a great part of the time talking to himself; but only like an unreasoning wheel, which also hummingly talks to itself; or rather, his body was a sentry-box and this self-talker on guard there, and talking all the time to keep himself awake.
